info.bio:
Gordon Matthew Sumner, (nacido el 2 de octubre de 1951), más conocido por su nombre artístico Sting, es un músico inglés anteriormente bajista, cantante y líder del grupo musical The Police.

Sting nació el 2 de Octubre de 1951 en Wallsend (Newcastle, Inglaterra). Hijo de un lechero, fue educado en la religión católica. Desde temprana edad supo que quería ser músico. Asistió a la Universidad de Warwick en Coventry, aunque no llegó a titularse.

scenes.name: Cantautores de los ochenta
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Absorbida la new wave, el mundo de los cantautores no vuelve a ser el mismo: los referentes pasan a ser Dylan, Neil Young, Cohen, Tim Buckley y Joni Mitchell. Las mujeres recuperan su estatus de seres filosóficos: Phranc, Suzanne Vega, Tracy Chapman, Melissa Etheridge, Michelle Shocked, Barbara Manning, Lucinda y Victoria Williams, Indigo Girls y, en Canadá, Jane Siberry, Mary Margaret O'Hara y Sarah McLachlan. Excéntricos: Jandek, Daniel Johnston, David Thomas, Alejandro Escovedo; en California, Stan Ridgway, Chris Isaak y Smog. En Gran Bretaña, Billy Bragg, Robyn Hitchcock, Julian Cope y, la voz más importante de la década, Nick Cave, predicador del apocalipsis moral (From Her To Eternity, The Good Son). Sinéad O'Connor, Sting, Morrissey, Momus; el pop celta de Enya y Loreena McKennitt; al cambiar la década, Joe Henry, Daniel Lanois y Bob Mould.

podcast.title: MTV Slogan Co-Writing Credit (1985)
podcast.body: Sting earned a co-songwriting credit on Dire Straits' "Money for Nothing" not just for his harmony vocals on the chorus, but for an additional vocal refrain he added to the front and back of the track. This refrain was a riff on "I want my MTV," a slogan he and The Police had used in an MTV ad years earlier, sung to the tune of The Police's "Don't Stand So Close To Me" as an inside joke. "He rift on the slogan that he and the police had yelled in that MTV ad a couple of years earlier, I want my MTV."

podcast.title: "Russians" Lyric Controversy (1986)
podcast.body: The core lyric of Sting's anti-nuclear lament "Russians," "if the Russians love their children too," was pilloried by some critics for its perceived glibness. Sting countered in interviews that he understood Russians loved their children, and the lyric was intended to be hyperbolic to emphasize the absurdity of nuclear war. "A lyric that some critics pilloried for its glibness in interviews Sting countered that of course he knew the Russians loved their children, and the lyric was meant to be hyperbolic to emphasize the absurdity of nuclear war."

podcast.title: Financial Impact of "Shape of My Heart" Samples (Post-1993)
podcast.body: Although "Shape of My Heart" was not a significant hit when released in 1993, its enduring appeal as a sample source, particularly for Juice Wrld's "Lucid Dreams," has generated millions of dollars. Sting shares the publishing on the song with his long-time guitarist Dominic Miller, who created the core guitar riff. "Sting has quipped in interviews that Lucid Dreams will put his grandkids through college, because it is built out of a sample of shape of my heart, a track from his lushly romantic 1993 album, Ten Summoners Tales."

podcast.title: Sting Endorses Bruno Mars' "Police" Imitation (2013)
podcast.body: Despite not receiving payment for Bruno Mars' 2012 hit "Locked Out of Heaven," which was a style imitation of The Police rather than a sample or interpolation, Sting endorsed the song. He even joined Mars on stage at the 2013 Grammy Awards to perform "Locked Out of Heaven" during a medley of reggae-inspired hits. "And as far as anyone knows, Sting wasn't paid a penny for Bruno Mars' hit, but Sting did endorse it."

podcast.body: As a teenager, Gordon Sumner would speed up records (33 RPM at 45 RPM, or 45s at 78) to better discern and learn the bass lines played by musicians such as Paul McCartney, James Jamerson, and Jack Bruce. podcast.title: Sting's Audience Shift (1990s)
podcast.body: After the "Ten Summoners Tales" album in 1993, Sting's audience increasingly shifted to adult contemporary. While college radio, alternative, and even some mainstream rock stations largely stopped playing his music, this "AC Sting" mode proved to be his most popular long-term, with his songs becoming staples on adult contemporary radio. "Sting's audience was always adult. Now it was primarily adult contemporary, with all the unhipped signifiers that indicated."

podcast.body: The widespread story that Sting engages in marathon sessions of tantric sex lasting for hours is completely false. This myth originated from a 1993 "Q Magazine" interview where a drunken Sting, prompted by Sir Bob Geldof, jokingly exaggerated his yoga practice, claiming it allowed him to "retain it all and go on for longer." Sting found the story hysterical and further modified it for fun, leading to the "eight hours at a time" detail, but it was all a lie. "I can take you to higher levels. Yeah, I started to use it to have sex. Now where you don't spill your seed, you retain it all and go on for longer and you never lose control and you just keep going."

podcast.title: Tree Frog Species
podcast.body: A species of tree frog, *Dendro's Sophos Sting-I*, was named after Sting when it was discovered in 1994. This naming honors Sting's significant efforts in conservation, specifically his work to protect the rainforests of South America. "This is a species of tree frog that was named after Sting when it was discovered in 1994. Why would they name it that? Well to honor Sting's efforts in trying to save the rainforests of South America, of course."

podcast.title: Ubiquity and Relevance
podcast.body: Sting grew accustomed to being ubiquitous, starting from The Police's breakthrough in the late 70s, and his ability to deliver mass appeal pop kept him on the charts into the 90s. His enduring sound and melodies have influenced Gen X, Millennial, and Gen Z artists who either borrowed his tunes directly or emulated his style. "He'd grown accustomed to being ubiquitous, ever since that former trio of his had broken out at the height of the UK punk scene in the late 70s."

xref.title: Attempted Murder-for-Hire Plot
xref.body: On May 7, 2013, Tim Lambesis was arrested in Oceanside, California, charged with attempting to hire a hitman to kill his wife. The plot originated when he discussed killing his wife with his steroid dealer at the gym, who then reported him to the police. Law enforcement set up a sting operation, where Lambesis met with an undercover detective. "On May 7, 2013, Lombicis was arrested in the Ocean Side, California. He was charged with trying to hire a hitman to kill the woman he wanted to divorce."

xref.title: Recruitment of Musicians for Band-Aid
xref.body: Bob Geldof initiated the Band-Aid project by reaching out to prominent musicians to create a charity single. His first call was to Midge Ure of Ultravox, followed by Sting of The Police, and Simon Le Bon of Duran Duran. As word spread, other notable artists such as Bono, David Bowie, and Paul Weller of The Jam, enthusiastically joined the effort, forming a supergroup of British talent. "First, he called mid-Jour of the band UltraVox. Sting of the police was called next, and Simon LeBawn of Durand Iran, and as words spread more people jumped on board."

xref.title: Sting Operation and Arrest Details
xref.body: During the sting operation, Tim Lambesis met with an undercover detective. He was arrested immediately after handing over the envelope in the parking lot of a Barnes and Noble bookstore.
